about: Wardrobe requirements for the townsfolk of Benevento, AD 700: every population group of src/npc/population.ts and every outfit profile of the v2 bodies (public/models/npc2). Rebuilt on 28 October 2026 (every group sourced on 29 October) after the earlier tools/npc3/wardrobe.json was lost with an uncommitted workspace; nothing here is copied from that file. Certainty: A attested (for this group, or for Lombard Italy in the 7th c.), I inferred from neighbouring evidence, H hypothesis/game choice. Narrative and limits: docs/npc/WARDROBE.md; groups: docs/benevento/PEOPLE.md.

PD.cite: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum IV 22 (dress of the earlier Lombards, from Theodelinda's paintings at Monza: loose garments, mostly linen, with broad borders woven in various colours; later trousers and leg wraps)

RB22.cite: Regula Benedicti 22: the monks sleep clothed and girded with belts or cords (cingulis aut funibus), without their knives at their sides

OR1.cite: Ordo Romanus I (late 7th / early 8th c. Roman papal ordo): the subdeacons bring the linen (alb), the girdle (cingulum), the amice, the dalmatics; English after Atchley

VEST.cite: Origins of ecclesiastical vestments: the girdled alb (linea) of Roman clergy

BELT.cite: Longobard belts as a typical, widespread component of dress for men and women; the early-7th-c. 'five-piece' bronze belt (buckle, tongue plate, strap end), later embellished with more plates and pendants (archaeometric study of Lombard belt fittings, Int. J. Metalcasting 2020)

MET.cite: Gold buckle and strap end, c. 600, from a Lombard horseman's grave associated with Castel Trosino (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

CASSANO.cite: Cassano d'Adda (Lombardy): bronze five-piece belt sets of the late 6th-early 7th c.; the seax usually hung from such belts (absent in those graves)

ROTILI.cite: M. Rotili, La necropoli longobarda di Benevento (1977): belt sets, disc brooches, gold-leaf crosses in Benevento's own Lombard graves (see docs/benevento/PEOPLE.md section 1)

VA.cite: V&A Egyptian tunic dated 670-870: an almost straight shirt-like tunic; belts gathered its folds (Egyptian analogue, not a Benevento find)

MET_TUNIC.cite: Met Kharga tunic, 4th-7th c.: cross-shaped, folded and sewn construction (Egyptian analogue)

ISID.cite: Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae XIX 33 'De cingulis' (c. 625): cinctus (wide), semicinctium, cingulum (narrowest); zona, the Greek name of the cingulum; XIX 22-25 on tunics

ROTH.cite: Edictum Rothari (643): the legal ranks of the Lombard kingdom (free arimanni, half-free aldii, servi), on which the poorer groups' plainer dress is inferred

RAV.cite: Ravenna mosaics, Sant'Apollinare Nuovo (6th c.): laymen in belted knee tunics, clergy in long girdled tunics, women in long tunics with mantles and veils

RAV2.cite: San Vitale, Ravenna: the court panels of Justinian and Theodora (c. 547), Byzantine lay and court dress

SMA.cite: Santa Maria Antiqua, Rome: wall paintings of the 7th and early 8th c. (John VII, 705-707): clergy and lay donors of the period in central Italy

BYZ.cite: Byzantine dress: the long tunic with a belt or sash for townsmen; women's long tunics with a girdle

WILL.cite: Huneberc, Hodoeporicon of St Willibald (c. 778): an English pilgrim's journey through Lombard Italy in the 720s (staff and scrip; ordinary travelling clothes)

VENOSA.cite: Jewish inscriptions of Venosa (5th-9th c.): a deeply Latinized community; no evidence of distinctive dress in this period

leather.geometry: strap 3.2 cm high, 4 mm thick, round the cinched waist; tongue 11 cm hanging from the buckle at the front
leather.fittings: buckle prop at the front (src/npc/population-props.ts makeBuckle): bronze frame and plate for Lombard men, a plain iron frame for townsmen; Lombard office-holders add the multi-part set of plates and strap ends (props.ts makeBeltFittings)
leather.certainty: A for Lombard men (five-piece and multi-part sets); I for Latin townsmen's plain belts

cord.geometry: round cord 1.2 cm thick, knotted at the front left with two ends (42 and 36 cm) hanging down the skirt
cord.material: hemp (unbleached, matte) for monks and the poor; white linen (cingulum) for priests and deacons
cord.certainty: A for monks (belts or cords) and for the clergy's girdle over the alb; the knot and the length of the ends are H

sash.geometry: woven band 4.2 cm wide, 3 mm thick, tied at the front left with two ends (34 and 28 cm)
sash.material: tabby wool or linen in the group's dye
sash.certainty: I: women's belts are attested in Lombard graves (often with buckles and pendants); a textile girdle is the inference for women whose graves keep no metal fittings and for Latin townswomen; the tied ends are H

cinch.rule: A belt draws the cloth in without changing the garment's dimensions: every edge of the garment keeps its length (99th percentile change <= 3 %, worst edge <= 20 %, judged per cm on sub-cm edges), the hem, neck and cuff perimeters within 1 %; the excess gathers and blouses above and below the belt. The 'belted-tunic study', which reshaped the panels, was rejected for exactly that.
cinch.fitted_exception: The gown's bodice is cut fitted at the waist: the girdle is tied over it and nothing is drawn in.

necklines.rule: No open, single-sided or see-through neckline: each neckline and sleeve cuff of a body garment has a turned-in facing (a 4 mm rim and a 2.5 cm inner band facing the body), drawn with the cloth's own material.
necklines.certainty: H: the exact finish is not documented for Benevento; turned and hemmed edges are the ordinary finish of woven garments (MET_TUNIC, VA).

garments: cloak with disc brooch at the right shoulder
belt (leather; hemp cord for slaves and beggars)
belt (leather, cingulum cord or sash by role)
robe.certainty: A for the clergy's girdled alb; I for the others

womanShawl.note: the v2 bodies have no separate shawl garment; this profile wears the veil only (open defect)

gasindus.fittings: multi-part set with the arms; spatha; seax when not cloaked

arimannus.fittings: multi-part set with spatha and seax

langobarda.fittings: disc brooch at the throat; belt pendants of the graves not modelled

bulgarus.people: Bulgar settled by Romuald (HL V 29), dressed as a Lombard freeman
bulgarus.fittings: with the arms: set, sword, seax

servus.note: hemp cord, worn and patched dress

faber.fittings: leather apron tied at the belt

presbyter.note: white linen cingulum over the alb

diaconus.note: white linen cingulum over the alb

monachus.note: belt or cord (RB 22); hemp cord chosen

iudaeus.people: Jewish dyer from Venosa, dressed like other townsmen

note_sources: Every group and outfit cites at least one source. Analogues (Ravenna, Rome, Egypt) show the dress of the wider late-antique and early-medieval Mediterranean, not Benevento itself; where a group's belt rests on them alone its certainty stays I or H.
